Content.Title: CEE MREL Watch: Let the asset class emerge!

Data.TextElement: It was inspiring to compare notes with the investor community at the CEE Banking Summit hosted by RBI earlier in June, which basically confirmed that MREL remains among pressing topics for the region. Now, as the deadline for legally-binding targets is drawing nigh (YE 2023), the origination of eligible bonds intensifies despite still rather issuer-unfriendly valuation for CEE risk on the international market. There is, however, a silver lining in this costly journey for the banks, which is the established visibility to global investors. The CEE FIG Eurobond segment has promptly developed from its infancy to a more mature stage reaching ~EUR 12 bn of debt outstanding in the public domain (≥EUR 250 mn size), which allows to treat it as a standalone asset class. Of course, this is still only a fraction of the western European banking universe, however here too, one can now enjoy a variety of investor choices. In this publication, we pore over the progress in CEE MREL issuance and also develop a composite (index) view of the sector.

Data.TextElement:
With the year-end deadline for MREL implementation approaching fast the CEE bank issuance of eligible liabilities mushrooms. By and large, the progress toward final legally-binding targets goes in line with our expectations (Fixed Income Watch CEE Banks: MREL race against the clock) showing new supply of MREL bonds (all asset classes and currencies) in excess of EUR 7 bn ytd, of which an equivalent of EUR 2.1 bn was squeezed into the pre summer break window in June. We see the banks to be generally well on track to close the remaining gaps in H2 2023, which should add another EUR 2-3 bn to the international and domestic public issuance per our estimate (still more of a topic for PL, HU and BG banks). The actual shortfall may be somewhat wider, but a cost-savvy approach would dictate the use of other means, including RWA optimization measures (e.g. synthetic securitization) and bilateral financing arrangements, both not without support by international financial institutions (IFIs). Furthermore, part of the financing need will be covered through internal capital generation (and retention).

Admittedly, the Eurobond market has been tough and costly for CEE banks notwithstanding their IG and/or national champion status, however there was little alternative to it in view of much more modest domestic investor base. We were positively surprised to what extent the banks could stretch their local borrowing capacities (again, thanks to IFIs), but even in this case the issuance in euro proved dominating at around EUR 12.5 bn in 2021-2023ytd, for almost 75% of the total external MREL bond placings in the region. In this regard, for CEE issuers previously lacking a proper track record on the international market this bond supply volume marked quite a rapid, even though difficult, development, so we can now assert that a full-scale debt market segment is born.

MREL issuance in CEE (EUR bn equiv.)
Source: Company data, Refinitiv, RBI/Raiffeisen Research
* External MREL bond issues (domestic and international); ** 1y before final maturity due to eligibility criteria

We emphasize that the issuance of MREL bonds is not a one-off exercise for CEE banks given that the prudential ratios shall be met at all times, i.e. the stock of eligible debt will have to be scaled up in line with any nominal RWA growth and adjusted to changes in capital buffer requirements. What is more to that, the uneasy market conditions of 2022/2023 made sure the flow of issuance will sustain in the near term on rollovers of the outstanding bonds due to their short originated tenors (3NC2 or 4NC3). We see the expected maturities for 2024 and 2025 at EUR 3-5 bn per annum, where the choice of marketplace/currency will be defined by prevailing monetary conditions and the appetite for CEE risk. Thus, borrowing on a local market short-term or at a floating rate might be sensible given a likely earlier reversion of the tightening cycle in CE/SEE as compared to the ECB. We note that non-euro players can generally secure better borrowing terms in local currencies, be it purely domestic bonds or a RegS format. In particular, this has been a case in point for Romanian and Polish banks (see chart below), which display a lower share of MREL issuance in foreign currency. In contrast to that, Hungary has trailed its peers in domestically-placed volumes though mainly due to a more acute need for size for the local market leader OTP (>EUR 2 bn of benchmark-size issues placed in 2022/2023). Notably, here too the bank tried to exploit cross-currency arbitrage opportunities, focusing on USD instruments (see for example OTP sticks with USD market for MREL).

MREL issuance 2021-2023ytd
Source: Company data, Refinitiv, RBI/Raiffeisen Research
Data per 30/06/2023
MREL issuance 2021-2023ytd
Source: Company data, Refinitiv, RBI/Raiffeisen Research
Data per 30/06/2023

Likewise, CEE banks are divided on the targeted class of MREL instruments, where individual bank-specific subordination requirement plays a key role. The latter aims at guarding against the no-creditor-worse-off (NCWO) risk and applies in the first place to system-relevant banks (referred to as “Pillar 1 Banks”). In case of CEE resolution entities, these are identified based on a quantitative criterion (total assets >EUR 100 bn) or at regulator's discretion. These "Top Tier Banks" are then subject to a minimum (Pillar I) subordination requirement of 13.5% TREA (plus the Combined Buffer Requirement) which may be further calibrated upward by the responsible authority if needed. Respectively, this appears to be a more relevant factor for larger and more concentrated CEE markets. Thus, the subordination requirement is basically forgone in Croatia and Slovakia allowing local banks to focus on cheaper Senior Preferred bonds. Alternatively, this is not the case in Poland, Czechia and Hungary where issuers have to tap lower-rank corners of the market, first and foremost the Senior Non-Preferred (SNP). Beyond that, individual capital planning and growth ambition can also drive tier 2 or AT1 issuance (e.g. related to M&A activity, as for OTP and NLB). No matter the targeted ranking, the banks prove eager to "sweeten" their offerings by adding an ESG label. The share of such issues has been especially high for Romanian and Slovakian banks (50-60%).

Given the heavy tilt toward either SP or SNP issues for single markets and issuers, it is still difficult to gauge a fair price discrepancy between the two classes in our region (as a reference, we currently see it at ~30-40bp for big Western banks). In this situation, a typical pecking order stands as only a secondary factor in the borrowing cost optimization — the main amount of savings is derived from a shrewd choice of the marketplace. To put things into perspective, CEE banks senior Eurobonds' issue spread (mid-swap) had seen a significant step-up after March 2022, which we estimate to be at least 200-250bp for BBB and 100-150bp for A-rated titles as compared to respective pre-war levels. Despite ebbs and flows and certain recovery in demand since then, the borrowing conditions on the international market remained generally unfriendly (see chart below). On the contrary, domestic investors would typically see intrinsic value differently, with an issue swap spread (EUR equivalent, IG CEE banks) rarely going above 250bp, which in some cases connotes an up to 250-300bp (!) differential in issuer's favor vs comparable Eurobond transactions. The banks explore all avenues to broaden their local investor base (private placements, retail format; cross-holdings of MREL instruments are generally regulated), but the capacity mainly suffices for smaller issue sizes (~EUR 100-120 mn on a rough average basis). This may well suit medium-size issuers, while larger players still have to go after deeper pockets of international investors.

CEE banks: international senior EUR bonds pricing
Source: Refinitiv, RBI/Raiffeisen Research
pagebreak

It is true that the forced oversupply of CEE MREL bonds has created an unfavorable technical backdrop for new issuers, but this does not seem to be the main problem for valuation. The market sentiment still has a keen bearing on the CEE risk pricing as it is basically stuck in the rut of the "proximity to war" premium concept, which has kept international investors rather lukewarm about the region. The banks thus have to vie for attention by offering juicy spreads, which, in turn, builds a track record that is then uneasy to disprove. Breaking this vicious circle is a challenge, however we think that the growing visibility to the international market further underpinned by a consistent story of solid performance may be of help here to whet investor appetite.

Fundamentally, CEE banks have stood their ground through 2022 reaping the full benefit of the high interest rate environment while keeping their cost of risk largely in check. With the reversion of monetary policies in CE/SEE likely unfolding cautiously (and possibly ahead of the ECB), the near-term outlook for banks' core revenues remains benign, although the net interest margin momentum is seen to wane amid catching-up deposit rates (and increasing flow to term deposits in the funding mix) and additional costly MREL financing. This should buffer the intensifying cost pressures (OPEX inflation, special taxes, country-specific litigation costs, etc.) and buttress pre-provisioning income. We note that the balance sheets might be tested for some "toxic" topics (e.g. commercial real estate), but asset quality risks are partly mitigated by low actual NPLs and accumulated management overlays. On a positive note, the region benefits from its conservative funding and liquidity profile featuring a stickier and more granular deposit base as compared to EU-average.

CEE banks' P&L drivers (median)*
Source: EBA, RBI/Raiffeisen Research
* For EBA sample of banks, based consolidated accounts

Source: EBA, RBI/Raiffeisen Research

A similar message we read from the credit rating drift (see below), which reveals only moderate bias toward downgrades in H2 2022 driven by idiosyncratic company risks and also negative rating action on respective governments. The track further showed some positive signs lately with few upgrades taking place in the CEE banking space in June 2023. In the context of debt capital markets, CEE banks hence build a segment of decent quality with an average rating anchored around the BBB grade; but to what extent they actually trade on these reasonable fundamentals?

CEE banks' rating drift*
Source: Refinitiv, RBI/Raiffeisen Research
* Simple count of changes in ST and LT foreign ratings and outlooks by S&P, Moody's, Fitch
CEE MREL Senior Eurobonds (EUR mn)*
Source: Refinitiv, RBI/Raiffeisen Research
* Principal amount outstanding for publicly placed EUR-denominated issues ≥EUR 300 mn in size

To give a quantitative answer to this question we develop a composite view of the CEE FIG bonds segment. Indeed, given the amassed volume of international issues, it fully deserves an own benchmark. We are not aware of any active index of this kind on the market currently, which adds a sense of novelty to the exercise. The strong gravity of the euro debt market for CEE issuers pretty much predetermines our focus on this single currency segment, where we consider CEE banks part of the global EUR FIG universe which we look at through the lens of the ICE BofA Euro family of indices. We hence borrow respective methodologies for the sake of comparability and overlay them on our third-party pricing sources (Refinitiv). The selection of bonds is based on the subordination (only SP and SNP rank), issue size (≥EUR 250 mn), remaining maturity (≥1y) and liquidity (no private placements) criteria which yield a sample of 27 eligible instruments as of July 2023 with EUR 10.9 bn principal amount outstanding and 3.2y average maturity. Naturally, the composite is populated by either foreign multiple point-of-entry (MPE) or local single point-of-entry (SPE) banking groups, which results in a significant weight of RBI and Erste's CEE subsidiaries (~50% based on face value) followed by OTP (~15%). In terms of the countries of risk, the custom index is more balanced with no single market exceeding 25% of the total. As a positive highlight, the region's strides toward sustainable financing are echoed in a nontrivial share of ESG-labeled issues (40% of the total), mainly green.

Principal amount outstanding
Source: Refinitiv, RBI/Raiffeisen Research
* Incl. CEE subsidiaries which are separate resolution entities
CEE EUR Senior Composite
Maturity profile (principal amount, EUR bn)*
Source: Refinitiv, RBI/Raiffeisen Research
* To the nearest call date

As mentioned, regulatory push toward the bail-in regime has been the major driver for CEE banks' bond issuance in the last years, which makes our CEE EUR Senior Composite basically an MREL index, where all bonds currently included represent bail-inable liabilities. Respectively, to satisfy one of the necessary MREL characteristics (≥1y remaining maturity) the bonds are typically callable one year prior to the final maturity date. In these circumstances, the banks' incentive to exercise the call option seems generally high, since the (expensive) funding would be losing its MREL powers otherwise. As a result, we take the yield to call as a conventional measure for our analysis. We construct this retrospectively with controls for a potential survival bias (which is relatively easy due to very limited presence of CEE banks on the Eurobond market in the pre-BRRD era).

The resulting picture (see below) confirms our hypothesis on the hefty premium the market currently assigns to CEE banks' senior unsecured risk. Measured by the yield spread to German Bunds, the segment trades at around 400bp, or ~230bp wide of the ICE BofA EUR Unsubordinated Financial index, which seems a step too far for a formal differential of one rating grade (BBB vs A, per our estimate). A distinct "after-war" valuation regime is also visible in a retrospective view illustrating the magnitude of the spread's blowup as compared to the preceding market phases characterized by CEE MREL early birds' entries (2021) and pre-BRRD bond supply (before 2021, represented mainly by top Polish lenders). Furthermore, the wide swings pertaining to the current stage underscore that investor sentiment may be fragile despite the tightening vibe lately. We note that the timing for normalization of the CEE risk premium is not clear while the reference to historical pre-war spread levels might be not exactly accurate due evolution of the constructed index (quadrupled number of constituents since YE 2021). Having said that, even without a durable spread compression CEE banks' senior Eurobonds offer enticing total return potential as we show in the next chapter.

Yield spread to benchmark curve (German Bunds) in bp
Source: Refinitiv, RBI/Raiffeisen Research
* The index contains CEE EUR-denominated senior bonds ≥EUR 250 mn size and ≥1Y residual maturity, market value-weighted

Cogent reasoning on the bonds' return potential warrants a more detailed view on valuation. For this purpose we perform a standard decomposition analysis of the projected holding period total return on a 6-month horizon, which can be split among:

  • Yield income (coupon return)
  • Rolldown (change in price due to passage of time assuming constant yield)
  • Change in price based on the assumed development of yields and yield spreads.

The first two return contributors are rather straightforward and can be directly derived from the bonds' characteristics. In this regard, the outlook on benchmark yields and spreads represents the crux of the matter, where we can further peel the onion by looking into the separate components of the: (i) risk-free rate (German Bunds), (ii) benchmark credit spread, and (iii) specific CEE bank premium over the benchmark. Starting with the top slice, we choose the EUR BBB Unsubordinated Bank sub-index (sub-sample of the ICE BofA Euro Unsubordinated Financial) as a refined benchmark. We do not stick to any outright trade scenario in this part, but rather look at the single CEE bonds total return sensitivities to a relative compression or widening of their pickup over the EUR BBB Unsubordinated Bank's spread curve by 20% (a reasonable value based on the recent historical volatility pattern, see previous chapter). Referring to the chart below for illustration, the proposed scenario analysis would keep the cloud of CEE banks' dots above the benchmark line, while making it more condensed coupled with a general move down (premium -20%) or more sparse in a move up (+20%). In this setup, the higher-yielding issues will be seeing proportionately stronger variation of the premium.

Relative valuation: CEE bank senior EUR bonds vs benchmark
Source: ICE BofAML, Refinitiv, RBI/Raiffeisen Research
* Sub-sample of the ICE BofA Euro Unsubordinated Financial index

Going further down the yield layers, our benchmark spread expectations are geared toward wider levels, including some +10-15bp penciled-in for the Financials Senior asset class till the year-end. Among the reasons behind is the outlook for risk-free rates which looks for a moderate downward trend in German Bund yields toward YE 2023 — on average, a 50-60bp setback for the 2y-5y section of the curve coupled with a steepening twist might be in the cards. In the environment of heightened rates volatility these two yield components are prone to technical counter-moves, i.e. a prompt rise in German Bund yields causes (temporary) tightening of the cash bond index spread and vice versa. For simplicity of presentation, we thus model it as a single yield change block uniformly applied to the selected CEE bonds, which we gauge at -30bp for the 6M horizon (more moderate than it is implied from the mentioned forecasts to reflect on the remaining uncertainty over the monetary path). It is true that the bull steepening move suggests a greater tightening effect on the front end, which we then deliberately neglect, but the resulting error should be mitigated by low duration of the affected instruments.

Within the outlined framework, CEE bank senior EUR bonds show quite robust results. Clearly, the combination of short maturities and high coupon inherent in 2022/2023 issues is investors' best friend. As presented on the chart below, holding period total return of ~3-4% (6M horizon) seems a reasonable guess for these instruments which have an additional bonus of low duration risk. Longer-dated and higher-yielding issues show greater earning potential (up to 7% in a favourable scenario). Although these are also more sensitive to a downside risk, the more pessimistic scenario of a deteriorating reception of CEE risk does not completely displace them either. This concerns not only the pre-2022 low-coupon issues largely reliant on the rolldown return, but also some of the more recent high-carry bonds trading strongly above par. Altogether, we find this story rather intriguing, so is it time for international investors to rethink the CEE bank Eurobonds risk in earnest?

Holding period total return potential, 6M horizon (selected CEE bank EUR bonds)
Source: Refinitiv, RBI/Raiffeisen Research
* Combined change in DE Bund yield and benchmark spread (EUR BBB Unsub. Banks): assumed at -30bp; ** Total return (TR) projection under scenarios for the spread over benchmark curve (EUR BBB Unsub. Banks): tightening by 20%, flat or widening by 20%

We note that the timing for normalization of the CEE risk premium is not clear while the reference to historical pre-war spread levels might be not exactly accurate due evolution of the constructed index (quadrupled number of constituents since YE 2021). Having said that, even without a durable spread compression CEE banks' senior Eurobonds offer enticing total return potential as we show in the next chapter.

Component.title: Total return expectations
Component.Data:
Cogent reasoning on the bonds' return potential warrants a more detailed view on valuation. For this purpose we perform a standard decomposition analysis of the projected holding period total return on a 6-month horizon, which can be split among:

  • Yield income (coupon return)
  • Rolldown (change in price due to passage of time assuming constant yield)
  • Change in price based on the assumed development of yields and yield spreads.

The first two return contributors are rather straightforward and can be directly derived from the bonds' characteristics. In this regard, the outlook on benchmark yields and spreads represents the crux of the matter, where we can further peel the onion by looking into the separate components of the: (i) risk-free rate (German Bunds), (ii) benchmark credit spread, and (iii) specific CEE bank premium over the benchmark. Starting with the top slice, we choose the EUR BBB Unsubordinated Bank sub-index (sub-sample of the ICE BofA Euro Unsubordinated Financial) as a refined benchmark. We do not stick to any outright trade scenario in this part, but rather look at the single CEE bonds total return sensitivities to a relative compression or widening of their pickup over the EUR BBB Unsubordinated Bank's spread curve by 20% (a reasonable value based on the recent historical volatility pattern, see previous chapter). Referring to the chart below for illustration, the proposed scenario analysis would keep the cloud of CEE banks' dots above the benchmark line, while making it more condensed coupled with a general move down (premium -20%) or more sparse in a move up (+20%). In this setup, the higher-yielding issues will be seeing proportionately stronger variation of the premium.

Relative valuation: CEE bank senior EUR bonds vs benchmark
Source: ICE BofAML, Refinitiv, RBI/Raiffeisen Research
* Sub-sample of the ICE BofA Euro Unsubordinated Financial index

Going further down the yield layers, our benchmark spread expectations are geared toward wider levels, including some +10-15bp penciled-in for the Financials Senior asset class till the year-end. Among the reasons behind is the outlook for risk-free rates which looks for a moderate downward trend in German Bund yields toward YE 2023 — on average, a 50-60bp setback for the 2y-5y section of the curve coupled with a steepening twist might be in the cards. In the environment of heightened rates volatility these two yield components are prone to technical counter-moves, i.e. a prompt rise in German Bund yields causes (temporary) tightening of the cash bond index spread and vice versa. For simplicity of presentation, we thus model it as a single yield change block uniformly applied to the selected CEE bonds, which we gauge at -30bp for the 6M horizon (more moderate than it is implied from the mentioned forecasts to reflect on the remaining uncertainty over the monetary path). It is true that the bull steepening move suggests a greater tightening effect on the front end, which we then deliberately neglect, but the resulting error should be mitigated by low duration of the affected instruments.

Within the outlined framework, CEE bank senior EUR bonds show quite robust results. Clearly, the combination of short maturities and high coupon inherent in 2022/2023 issues is investors' best friend. As presented on the chart below, holding period total return of ~3-4% (6M horizon) seems a reasonable guess for these instruments which have an additional bonus of low duration risk. Longer-dated and higher-yielding issues show greater earning potential (up to 7% in a favourable scenario). Although these are also more sensitive to a downside risk, the more pessimistic scenario of a deteriorating reception of CEE risk does not completely displace them either. This concerns not only the pre-2022 low-coupon issues largely reliant on the rolldown return, but also some of the more recent high-carry bonds trading strongly above par. Altogether, we find this story rather intriguing, so is it time for international investors to rethink the CEE bank Eurobonds risk in earnest?

Outside the working hours, Ruslan’s family is a priority, though in the rare minute of free time he might enjoy playing guitar or a game of chess.

Thomas Leirer studied banking and finance and has been an analyst in the Fixed Income & ESG Team at Raiffeisen Research since 2022. Joerg leads the Fixed Income & ESG Research department.
